newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank leaders unite to defend ECB neutrality.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank leaders unite to defend ECB neutrality.

text.p: Council members at Germany's Bundesbank may have disparate views on the economic need for interest rate cuts, but they have united to drive home the view that Europe's central bank must be free of all political influence.

In speeches over the last few weeks, top Bundesbank officials have launched a relentless attack on attempts to undermine the political neutrality of the authority designated as the guardian of Europe's single currency.

At the root of their worries is a fear that the strongly-worded clauses on central bank independence in the Maastricht Treaty may lose force if individual governments start to take them less seriously or offer new interpretations.

The fact that Germany's closest European ally, France, has been at the forefront of the political wavering has led some officials to suggest that deep-seated differences with Paris could present an obstacle to the euro's success.

Speaking in Bonn on Wednesday, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer made clear that there was no room for compromise over the central bank's independence and that even a hint that this was being accepted reluctantly could harm its credibility.
"The dangers of the proposed European System of Central Banks having an independence which is accepted only formally and reluctantly should also not be underestimated," he said.
"A hidden dissent could place a considerable burden on the necessary credibility of the European Central Bank, not to speak of the monetary union's later susceptibility to conflict," he added.

Tension over the central bank's impartiality was first stirred late last year, when French officials began to worry that the exchange rate would in future effectively be dictated by the actions of a supranational, monetarist authority -- a clear break with France's tradition of ultimate state control.
The Bundesbank's leaders, imbued with the conviction that the fight against domestic inflation is paramount, balked at the comments, dealing out a barrage of criticism to the French.
Helmut Hesse, striking where it hurt, said the French were maybe just unwilling to give up sovereignty on some issues.
Reimut Jochimsen stressed that differences with Paris had to be ironed out now, before the 1999 start of monetary union.
And Olaf Sievert dismissed out of hand an original French proposal to create a political counterweight to the European Central Bank, which could also act as a currency rate watchdog.

"Of course, once the European Central Bank has the power to take the role which the Maastricht Treaties have given it, there may be some comfort in the fact that a stability council, which has nothing to decide, would only make a fool of itself if it hit on the idea of suggesting that the moon should go in the opposite direction from that which is ordained," he said.

Even Tietmeyer, who as Bundesbank president speaks for the council as a whole, made an unusual foray into the French language for a direct attack on proposals that a "pouvoir politique" (political power) should counter the "pouvoir monetaire" (monetary power).

The only word of encouragement, with strong conditionality attached, came on Thursday from Bundesbank deputy president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum in response to a watered-down French plan to establish an informal gathering of ministers of euro countries, with no decision-making power.

Echoing a view expressed by European Monetary Institute president Alexandre Lamfalussy this week, Gaddum told the Handelsblatt newspaper that France's proposal for a stability council could be welcomed if the council's aim was to co-ordinate efforts toward monetary stability.
